food.text: Between 9000 BCE and 5000 BCE, Niger-Congo speakers independently developed agriculture in West Africa, with yams among the crops. Oil palm and raffia palm were domesticated as early as 9000 BCE.

Between 9000 BCE and 5000 BCE, Niger-Congo speakers in West Africa independently developed agriculture. Yams were among their early crops. Farming was not simply imported into the region but grew from local experiments with native plants.
Between 8000 BCE and 6000 BCE, Nilo-Saharan speakers in the steppes and savannah of the Sahara and Sahel began to collect and domesticate wild millet and sorghum.

At Ounjougou, Mali, Niger-Congo speakers made mature pottery before 9400 BCE and used it to hold and cook grains. Two of the grains named are Digitaria exilis and pearl millet. This is part of the earliest pottery in Africa.
West African farmers domesticated two seed plants, black-eyed peas and voandzeia (African groundnuts). Okra and kola nuts were domesticated afterward, adding to a growing set of local crops.
Oil palm and raffia palm were domesticated as early as 9000 BCE in West Africa. Both came from the wetter, expanding rainforest and wooded savannah that stretched from Senegal to Cameroon.

Two seed plants, black-eyed peas and voandzeia (African groundnuts), were domesticated in prehistoric West Africa. Okra and kola nuts followed. Before 5000 BCE these farming practices spread through the woodland savanna, and afterward they moved south into the forest.
Most of the early West African crops grew in the forest. Niger-Congo speakers therefore invented polished stone axes for clearing it. Farming here needed new tools as well as new plants.

Later, people in the Sahara and Sahel also collected and domesticated gourds, watermelons, castor beans and cotton. These crops followed the earlier domestication of wild millet and sorghum by Nilo-Saharan speakers.
In the Sahara and Sahel, people began capturing wild cattle and holding them in circular thorn hedges. Keeping the animals penned in this way led to their domestication.

In 4000 BCE, during the Pastoral Period of the Sahara, herders developed a more sophisticated social structure, including the trade of cattle as valued assets. Herds of livestock had become a form of wealth.

Before 5000 BCE, West African farming practices spread throughout the woodland savanna. Afterward they were introduced southward into the West African forest, carrying the new way of life into new landscapes.

Ethnographically and historically, West African women have been the makers of pottery in most West African ceramic traditions. The craft is closely associated with creativity and fertility. The earliest known West African pottery, at Ounjougou, was used to cook grains.

art.text: Pottery made at Ounjougou in Mali is the earliest pottery in Africa, dating to at least 9400 BCE. Niger-Congo speakers are described as having invented it independently. They later carried their pottery into the Central Sahara.

Wavy-line and dotted wavy-line pottery, decorated with rippling lines, spread from Mauritania all the way to the Red Sea. This wide distribution supports the conclusion that the regions traded with one another and were interconnected.

Wavy-line and dotted wavy-line pottery were produced between the 8th and 4th millennia BCE, in the Saharan-Sahelian and Middle Nile Valley regions. This decorated pottery came before the emergence of monarchic tumuli, the burial mounds of later rulers.

Before 9400 BCE, Niger-Congo speakers at Ounjougou in Mali were already using mature ceramic technology. They made pots to contain and cook grains such as Digitaria exilis and pearl millet, and they had also developed pyrotechnology by the 10th millennium BCE.

Dotted wavy-line pottery spread across the Ennedi Plateau, the Niger Plateau and Wadi Howar in the Saharan-Sahelian region. In doing so it linked the Middle Nile River, Lake Chad and the Benue-Niger River.
Tumuli with megalithic monuments developed as early as 4700 BCE in the Saharan region of Niger. They may have served as antecedents for the mastabas and pyramids of ancient Egypt.

science.text: At Ounjougou in Mali, Niger-Congo speakers independently created pottery by at least 9400 BCE, the earliest pottery in Africa. They used it to contain and cook grains such as fonio and pearl millet.
Between 9000 BCE and 5000 BCE, Niger-Congo speakers in West Africa independently developed agriculture, including the growing of yams. Oil palm and raffia palm were domesticated as early as 9000 BCE.

Because most of the crops grew in the forest, Niger-Congo speakers invented polished stone axes to clear it. Their farming practices had spread through the woodland savanna before 5000 BCE and were afterward carried southward into the West African forest.

Around 9500 BCE the Sahara was far more humid than today, and the Niger River formed a vast inland lake near Timbuktu and Araouane. Northern Mali then resembled the savannah of southern Mali today, until increasing aridity set in around 5000 BCE.

In the 10th millennium BCE, Niger-Congo speakers at Ounjougou, Mali, developed pyrotechnology. Their people were also using independently invented bows and arrows as they moved into the Central Sahara.

Ceramics at Ounjougou in central Mali have been dated to around 9400 BCE, one of the earliest known examples in West Africa. At the Ravin de la Mouche site, part of the Ounjougou complex, dates between 11,400 and 10,200 years ago have been recorded.

Niger-Congo speakers, possibly accompanied by wild helmeted guineafowls, may have moved into West Africa and domesticated the birds by 3000 BCE. This would make the guineafowl one of the region's early domesticated animals.

The sickle cell mutation originated in the Sahara or in western Central Africa by at least 7,300 years ago, though possibly as early as 22,000 years ago. The ancestral haplotype may have first arisen in the ancestors of modern West Africans. Sickle cell disease is one of the genetic adaptations to malaria found among Sub-Saharan Africans, alongside the Duffy blood group and increased rates of G6PD deficiency, and the malaria adaptation may have first developed around 7300 BP.

culture.text: Niger-Congo speakers at Ounjougou, Mali, independently created pottery by at least 9400 BCE. It is the earliest pottery known in Africa, and it appeared in West Africa without being borrowed from elsewhere.

West African hunter-gatherers lived throughout coastal West Africa by 12,000 BP. Between 12,000 BP and 8000 BP they migrated northward as far as Mali, Burkina Faso, and Mauritania, so people were moving across the region long before farming spread.

At Ounjougou, Niger-Congo speakers used pottery to contain and cook grains such as Digitaria exilis and pearl millet before 9400 BCE. They had also developed pyrotechnology there in the 10th millennium BCE.
Niger-Congo speakers carried bows and arrows they had invented independently, along with their pottery, into the Central Sahara. By 10,000 BP it had become their primary region of residence.

Around 4000 BCE, herders in the Sahara's Pastoral Period began to develop a sophisticated social structure, including trade in cattle as valued assets. Their culture left behind fields of tumuli, lustrous stone rings, and axes.
In the late 10th to early 9th millennium BCE, the creators of the Ounjougou pottery in Mali — the earliest pottery in Africa — migrated with their pottery from Ounjougou into the Central Sahara.

The Holocene Wet Phase brought expanding rainforest and wooded savannah from Senegal to Cameroon. Since most of the crops grew in the forest, Niger-Congo speakers invented polished stone axes to clear it.
The Dufuna canoe was built about 8000 years ago in northern Nigeria. It is the second earliest form of water vessel known in Sub-Saharan Africa.
